title: Trent on grace
hook: justification begins with grace, received in faith, and bears fruit in works

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vulgate, and the books listed by name. Your line was the whole canon. Did you read a passage you usually skip? Day seven hundred eighty-six.

Two lines, one Bible. Paul writes to the Ephesians, in the Douay-Rheims, "For by grace you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, for it is the gift of God." James writes, "faith without works is dead." Read either one alone and it can sound like the whole story. The reformers leaned hard on Paul, and some of them were uneasy with James. At Trent, the bishops spent a long time trying to hold both lines in one hand. Today's title is Trent on grace.
screen: `PAUL: BY GRACE, THROUGH FAITH.` → `JAMES: FAITH WITHOUT WORKS IS DEAD.` → `BOTH IN ONE HAND.`

segments.voice: The council's decree on justification, being made right with God, moves in a careful order. First, grace begins it. The decree says the beginning comes from God's grace, which goes ahead of us and calls us without any merit of our own. We don't start the journey. God does. Second, faith receives it. The decree calls faith the beginning of human salvation, the foundation and root of all justification. And it adds a striking line: nothing that comes before justification, neither faith nor works, earns the grace of justification. It's a gift. Third, it bears fruit. For Trent, justification isn't only having sins forgiven. It's being made new on the inside. And a person who's been made new grows, and that growth shows in love and in works. That's where James comes in: works aren't the price of grace. They're what grace does when it's alive in someone. Then, the guardrail. Among its canons, the council condemned the idea that a person can be made right with God by their own works, without God's grace through Christ. Some people imagine Catholics believe you earn your way to God. Trent rules that out: good works matter, but they grow from grace, never apart from it. Catholics and Lutherans still differ on how this works in a person. But the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation have since signed a joint declaration saying they share a basic understanding of justification by grace. That's today's line: grace first.
screen: `FIRST: GRACE GOES AHEAD.` · `SECOND: FAITH, THE ROOT.` · `THIRD: GRACE BEARS FRUIT.` · `NO ONE EARNS IT BY WORKS.` · then, large: `GRACE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank God for grace first, or, if you don't pray, just notice it. Use the sit. Bring to mind three good things in your life you didn't earn. A meal someone else cooked. Someone who loved you before you'd done anything. A morning you were given. Let each one sit for a few breaths. Don't turn them into a to-do list. Just receive them. If you pray, you can say thank you, simply, once for each. Then, at the end, notice whether anything in you wants to give something back. The bell holds the time.
Justification. Trent's teaching that being made right with God begins with grace, is received in faith, and bears fruit in works. Today's word.
Your line: grace first. Today, before you do the good thing you're planning, pause and name what was given to you first. Day seven hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics are taught that justification begins with God's grace, given in baptism, received in faith and growing through love and good works; the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation have signed a joint declaration on the doctrine of justification.

notes: Session VI paraphrased: ch. 5 (prevenient grace, 'without any existing merits'), ch. 7 (not remission of sins only but sanctification and renewal of the inward man), ch. 8 (faith 'the beginning of human salvation, the foundation and root of all justification'; 'none of those things which precede justification, whether faith or works, merit the grace itself of justification'), canon 1. Confirm.
'The bishops spent a long time' on the decree: kept vague under the claims rule; confirm.
'Their opponents were accused of leaning on James' (Luther's view of James): confirm fairness, or Keeper may simplify.
Joint Declaration (1999; year not spoken) described as 'in recent decades' and 'a basic understanding of justification'; confirm wording.
'Some people imagine Catholics believe you earn heaven' names a misconception, not any tradition's teaching; confirm tone.
Practice says 'three good things': a count for the listener's own practice, not a factual claim.
Editor: replaced the garbled 'opponents were accused of leaning on James'; dropped 'in recent decades'; swapped the breath-as-gift image (used day 771) for a meal.
Editor 2: hook line 'you might build a whole religion on it' replaced, as it could read as a jab at the reformers.

Audit: 'Trent says the opposite' (of earning heaven) overstated; Trent also teaches merit and eternal life as reward (Session VI ch. 16, canon 32), so the line now says works grow from grace, never apart from it.
